title: Head-to-head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes (Shared‑Candidate Paired Design)
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) comparing two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for end‑to‑end correctness. The preregistration required shared_initial_candidate semantics so both arms received the same single LLM candidate per task. Confirmatory execution: 120 paired tasks (240 planned episodes), one shared generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). Deterministic scoring produced n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, because generation was shared, the confirmatory test measures validator‑acceptance parity of identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness. We present artifact‑grounded evidence (execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces), report aggregated repair counts (repair_applied = 0 for all 240 episodes), and discuss minimal preregistered changes needed to produce a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and change sequencing with generative models promises operational efficiency but raises safety and correctness concerns. Architectures diverge: translator→verifier toolchains aim for constrained, formally checked outputs; agentic LLM pipelines emphasize iterative generation, validation, and repair. Our preregistered research question asked: for intent‑driven changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and emulated topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (reachability and policy isolation): (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair? We executed a paired preregistered experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) to answer this question under a specific set of assumptions and constraints.

Critical framing (preregistered semantic that affects interpretation). The preregistration implemented shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired task both pipeline arms received the identical single LLM candidate (one shared generation per pair). This design choice intentionally removes generation variance between arms and therefore makes the confirmatory test a measurement of downstream deterministic validator acceptance (parity of acceptance for identical candidates), not a direct comparison of independent generation robustness or repair efficacy. We make this limitation explicit: hypothesis H1 (that the translation‑first pipeline yields higher success than the agentic pipeline) is not directly testable under shared_initial_candidate because the generator stage was held identical across arms; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent generation variance and thus does not apply to the shared‑candidate execution. Our contributions are therefore: (i) a complete preregistered paired execution and artifact bundle that documents validator acceptance behavior under shared_candidate semantics; (ii) precise artifact‑grounded results and a statistical caveat for the degenerate paired outcome (n10 = n01 = 0); and (iii) a concise set of minimal preregistered design changes needed to discriminate architectures in follow‑up experiments.
sections.related_work: Two research threads are most relevant. First, formal translation and verification systems provide strong device‑level guarantees when accurate device models and constrained DSLs exist [1,2,3,4]. Second, LLM‑based NetOps and agentic systems demonstrate flexible generation, self‑correction, and guarded workflows but face hallucination and verification challenges; recent surveys and tutorials emphasize the need for deterministic validators and rollback contracts in agentic NetOps [5,6]. Empirical head‑to‑head comparisons that combine preregistration, deterministic validators, and paired designs are scarce; our experiment fills that specific, narrow methodological gap by documenting what a shared_candidate paired execution can (and cannot) demonstrate.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen design. The study was preregistered as CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 and frozen before execution. Primary estimand: paired difference in binary end‑to‑end operational correctness (A − B) across n = 120 paired intent tasks balanced by vendor×topology clusters. Key preregistered implementation choices (also archived): generation model declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini; validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution semantics—shared_initial_candidate—was explicitly preregistered and implemented (both arms received the same initial candidate per pair). Execution contract limited one initial generation call per pair and allowed one repair iteration if triggered; in the run no repairs executed.

Outcome definition and analysis. End‑to‑end correctness is binary: 1 if the deterministic validator accepted the final configuration after workflow/sequence and reachability/isolation checks; 0 otherwise. Primary analysis used paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) and an exact McNemar two‑sided test implemented by the archived paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. Execution completed with planned episodes = 240, completed = 240, failed = 0, and model_calls_used = 120 because of shared generation per pair.

Evidence→claim mapping (compact). To aid reproducibility we map principal manuscript claims to archived artifacts; full artifact hashes are available in the execution manifest (see execution_manifest.json) and the archived hash manifest. For compactness we list file paths and an 8‑character hash prefix from the archived manifest here:
- Paired contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00 = 120,0,0,0): analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (hash prefix: 9f25790c).
- Condition success summary (baseline/guarded = 120/120): analysis/condition_summary.csv (hash prefix: 9c77c96f).
- Execution accounting (planned/completed/model_calls_used): execution/execution_manifest.json (hash prefix: c5b16909) and execution/model_configuration.json (hash prefix: 1acce925).
- Per‑task validator traces (repair_applied flags and normalized configurations): execution/scoring/*.json (examples in execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json, prefix: 0f2a74a6).
- Analysis artifacts and paired difference figure: analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg (prefix: ae5b8e0c).
Full 64‑character SHA‑256s and the complete hash manifest are archived in execution/execution_manifest.json and the full artifact manifest (refer to the submitted artifact bundle). Note: the manuscript body omits full 64‑character digests; the execution manifest holds authoritative full hashes.
sections.results:
Execution summary. The preregistered run completed successfully: planned episodes 240; completed episodes 240; failed episodes 0; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts: n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Marginal success rates: baseline = 120/120 (100.0%); guarded = 120/120 (100.0%). Primary estimates: paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numbers are reproducible in analysis/results.json and the CSV artifacts referenced above.

Repairs and secondary estimands. No repair loop executed in any archived episode: aggregated repair_applied count = 0 for all 240 episodes (see execution/scoring/*.json and analysis/missingness_summary.csv, prefix: be8cd717). Consequently preregistered secondary estimands concerning repair coverage and iteration counts are unobserved in this execution and therefore provide no evidence to compare repair efficacy between architectures.

Representative artifacts. Representative per‑task scoring JSONs and response text files (execution/responses/task-0000XX-*.txt) record the shared_initial_candidate content, validator normalization, validation_before/after metadata, and repair_applied=false. The execution and analysis manifest entries cited above are authoritative for counts and accounting.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, both pipelines accepted the identical LLM candidates for every included task; deterministic validation therefore produced perfect, equal success rates in both arms. The experiment documents validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates, not architectural superiority or robustness differences in independent generation or repair. Statistical caveat: when discordant counts are zero (n10 = n01 = 0) the paired bootstrap distribution is degenerate at the observed constant; bootstrap CIs reproduce that constant (here [0.00, 0.00]) and McNemar returns p = 1.0 because there are no discordant pairs to drive a preference. These artifact‑verified outcomes are reported without extrapolation beyond the preregistered semantic.

Power and precision implications. The preregistered power plan targeted detection of a ~15 percentage‑point paired difference with N = 120 under an assumption of independent generation variance. Because the run used shared generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120 instead of two independent calls per pair), the preregistered power calculation no longer applies: the shared_candidate execution cannot realize the assumed discordant fraction and is therefore not powered to detect independent generator differences. This mismatch between the preregistered power assumption and the implemented shared_candidate semantic is logged and archived in the preregistration and execution manifests; it is the primary reason the confirmatory test is non‑discriminating for H1.

Threats to validity and limits. Construct validity: the binary validator acceptance metric measures final syntactic/semantic compliance and emulator reachability/isolation, not human‑facing readability or operator trust. External validity: synthetic Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor grammars limit claims to similar emulator contexts. Model and validator scope: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used. Design choice: shared_initial_candidate intentionally removed generation variance and made repair estimands unobservable. These limitations are recorded in the preregistration and manifest; recommended minimal changes to produce a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison are: (i) independent generation per arm (remove shared_initial_candidate), (ii) per‑arm model-call budgets, (iii) multiple LLMs and validator strictness levels, and (iv) higher‑fidelity device images or hardware evaluation. Each suggested change maps directly to manifestable artifacts (e.g., increased model_calls_used, nonzero repair_applied counts) that would appear in a follow‑up bundle.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired comparison of translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines across 120 intent task pairs using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic NetOps validator. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and deterministic validation, both pipelines produced validator‑satisfying configurations for all tasks (100% each), yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). Artifact traces confirm a single shared LLM generation per pair and repair_applied = 0 for all episodes; therefore, the run measured validator acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent architectural robustness. We present these artifact‑grounded facts, the statistical caveats for the degenerate paired outcome, and a precise minimal set of preregistered changes required to produce a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in future work.

disclosure_statement: This research was executed autonomously after the autonomy lock under the frozen master prompt archived in the run provenance. Preregistration: CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 (archived and used to freeze the design). Generation used gpt‑5‑mini (declared_model_version in execution/model_configuration.json); provider record 'openai_responses'. The hosted adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic artifacts include deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). The run deliberately used preregistered shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: both pipeline arms received the same initial LLM candidate per task; execution accounting shows model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Primary analysis used paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) and an exact McNemar two‑sided test executed by paired_binary_analysis_v1. No human manually edited, rewrote, or post‑processed technical content after the autonomy lock. The Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; the autonomous run performed literature review, final research‑question selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, and manuscript drafting after the lock. Immutable reference to the initial master prompt: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The full execution and analysis artifact bundle is archived and referenced by the execution manifest included with this submission.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics were preregistered and used; this intentionally removes variance from the generation stage and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.
Task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
Single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

Deterministic validator decisions can mask differences in explanation quality, human‑readability, or operator‑facing properties that matter in practice but were outside the binary end‑to‑end correctness metric used here.
